About: a star held up by gas pressure, contracting as it radiates with no nuclear source

About this simulation

On screen
Left: the star drawn to scale on a frame reaching 11 R☉ from its centre, with a dashed circle the size of the present Sun and a faint ring at the starting radius of 10 R☉. The colour of the disc shows the mean interior temperature on a fixed log scale from 0.2 MK (deep red) to 3 MK (white), with a key in the corner. Wavy arrows leave the surface while the radiation is on. Right: the thermal energy Eth (light grey, up), the gravitational energy Egrav (dark grey, down) and the total energy Etot (blue, down) on a fixed axis from −25 to +25 × 1040 J, with thin outlines of the bars at t = 0.
Controls
Radiation switches the loss of energy at the rate L☉ on and off. γ chooses the ratio of heat capacities of the gas (5/3, 3/2 or 1.4) and returns the star to its start, with the radiation off. ⏮ Rewind returns the star to 10 R☉ with the radiation off and the clock at zero; the header ↻ Reset also restarts the current mode.
Measured
The clock runs at 0.3 million years of star time per second while the radiation is on. A uniform-density star of one solar mass with μ = 0.61, contracting through equilibrium states at constant L = L☉; energies in units of 1040 J, temperature in million kelvin. The run stops at 1 R☉. The time, radius, mean temperature, energy radiated and rise in thermal energy are in the Readouts panel of the sidebar.
When it holds
The negative heat capacity, C = −(3γ − 4)NkB/(γ − 1), needs the star to stay in virial equilibrium, contracting slowly compared with its dynamical time, and to be held up by an ideal gas with γ above 4/3. A degenerate gas, or a star knocked out of equilibrium, does not behave this way. Uniform density and a constant L = L☉ are simplifications: a real contracting protostar is centrally condensed and its luminosity changes as it shrinks.

Guided Inquiry

1 · A star that radiates

Set γ to 5/3. The star starts at a radius of 10 R☉ with the radiation off. Before switching the radiation on, predict what happens to the mean temperature of the star as it loses energy. Then switch the radiation on and watch the glow and the temperature readout for about ten seconds.

2 · The three energy bars

Keep γ at 5/3; the star is back at 10 R☉. Before switching the radiation on, predict how the three energy bars change as the star radiates. Then switch the radiation on and compare the bars with their dashed starting outlines.

3 · Where the energy goes

Keep the settings of question 2 and let the star run. Before reading the readouts, predict what share of the gravitational energy released by the contraction is radiated away. Then compare the readouts of the energy radiated and of the rise in thermal energy.

4 · Temperature at half the radius

Keep γ at 5/3; the star is back at 10 R☉. You will switch the radiation on and watch the radius and the temperature readouts. Before you do, predict the mean temperature when the radius has fallen from 10 R☉ to 5 R☉, given that it starts at 0.28 million kelvin.

5 · A different gamma

Set γ to 1.4; the star starts again at 10 R☉. Before switching the radiation on, predict how this star behaves compared with the one at γ = 5/3, which started at the same radius. Then switch the radiation on and watch the total-energy bar, the radius and the clock.

6 · The energy budget again

Keep γ at 1.4; the star is back at 10 R☉. You will switch the radiation on and switch it off again when the energy radiated reaches about 1.0 × 1040 J, after about three seconds. Before you do, predict the rise in thermal energy the readout will show then.

7 · What you found

A star held up by gas pressure has a negative heat capacity: losing energy, it contracts and heats, with its mean temperature going as 1/R. The virial theorem fixes the budget: at γ = 5/3 half the gravitational energy released is radiated and half heats the gas; at γ = 1.4 only a sixth is radiated. This holds only while the star stays in virial equilibrium, contracting slowly, and is held up by an ideal gas with γ above 4/3; as γ → 4/3 the star becomes barely bound.

The Physics

A Star Shining Without Fuel · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A star with no nuclear fuel still shines. This sim follows a uniform star of one solar mass that starts at 10 solar radii and radiates at the Sun's rate, L⊙. It shows the star drawn to scale, its energies as three bars, and the mean temperature and radiated energy as readouts.

What you'll learn

  • What fixes a star's mean temperature.
  • Where the energy a star radiates comes from.
  • How the ratio of heat capacities, γ, changes the accounting.
The opening state, sketched: the star at 10 R⊙ with the Sun's size dashed, and the three energy bars.

What's on screen

  • The star, drawn to scale. Its colour is the mean interior temperature on a fixed scale from 0.2 MK (deep red) to 3 MK (white). The dashed circle is the present Sun, the faint ring is the starting radius of 10 R⊙, and wavy arrows leave the surface while the radiation is on.
  • Thermal Eth (light grey, up), gravity Egrav (dark grey, down) and total Etot (blue, down), on a fixed axis from −25 to +25 × 1040 J. Thin dashed outlines show the bars at t = 0.
  • Readouts: the time t, the radius R, the mean temperature, the energy radiated Erad and the rise in thermal energy ΔEth.
See itLook at the star before anything happens. Watch for: Radius reading 10.00 R⊙, the mean temperature 0.282 MK, and every bar sitting on its dashed outline.

03

A star that radiates gets hotter: the mean temperature is T̄ ∝ 1/R

Gas pressure holds the star up against its own gravity. For a gas whose ratio of heat capacities is γ, the balance is the virial theorem (notes 4.20):

Equation (4.20). For γ = 5/3 it reads 2Eth + Egrav = 0.

For a uniform star the virial theorem sets the thermal energy of M/μmH particles, (3/2)(M/μmH)kBT̄, equal to 3GM²/10R, which gives (4.23):

Equation (4.23). The sim's star has T̄ = 0.282 MK at 10 R⊙ and 2.82 MK at 1 R⊙.
Mean temperature against radius for the sim's star.

Radiating can only lower the total energy, and Etot is negative and proportional to 1/R. So a star that radiates must shrink, and the smaller R is, the larger T̄. Halving R doubles T̄, from 0.282 to 0.564 MK.

Key idea. Losing energy makes a star contract, and a contracting star is hotter: it has a negative heat capacity.
See itSwitch the radiation on at γ = 5/3 and stop when the radius has halved. Watch for: Radius reading 5.00 R⊙ and the mean temperature 0.564 MK, twice the start.
04

Half the released energy is radiated, half heats the gas

At γ = 5/3 the virial theorem fixes the total energy (4.22):

Equation (4.22), a negative total energy: the star is bound.

Radiating at L makes Etot fall at the rate L. So Egrav falls at 2L and Eth rises at L. Of the gravitational energy the contraction releases, half is radiated and half heats the gas (notes Figure 43).

The sim's star as R halves from 10 to 5 R⊙ (γ = 5/3).

At R = 5 R⊙, after 0.94 Myr, Erad and ΔEth both read 1.139 × 1040 J, while Egrav has fallen by 2.277. The luminosity sets how fast this happens, but not the split.

See itLet the star shine until its radius is a third of the start. Watch for: Radiated Erad and Thermal rise ΔEth both reading 2.277 × 1040 J, at 3.33 R⊙.
05

The split depends on the gas: Etot = (3γ − 4) Egrav / 3(γ − 1)

The gas sets the split through its ratio of heat capacities γ. For general γ, the relation 3(γ − 1)Eth = −Egrav gives (notes, after 4.23):

Negative only for γ above 4/3, and tending to zero as γ → 4/3: the star is only loosely bound.

Radiation, with energy density three times its pressure, acts as γ = 4/3. A smaller share of Egrav is radiated, so the rest heats the gas: ΔEth/Erad = 1/(3γ − 4). The same L⊙ then shrinks a loosely bound star faster.

06

Where it matters

  • Protostars. A star with no fuel but its own gravity heats its centre as it contracts, until the temperature at which fusion begins. The sim stops at 1 R⊙, where T̄ is 2.82 MK.
  • Stable burning. Run the argument backwards. A star whose reactions release energy faster than it radiates expands and cools, which slows the reactions.
  • The Kelvin–Helmholtz time. Gravity alone can supply the luminosity for tKH = |Egrav|/2L (4.24), about 107 yr for the Sun, far less than its 4.6 × 109 yr. The Sun must have another source: fusion. For the sim's star at 10 R⊙ it is 0.94 Myr, the time R takes to halve at γ = 5/3.
Go deeper: when the negative heat capacity holds
  • The thermal energy of the gas is N kBT/(γ − 1), so Etot = −(3γ − 4)Eth gives C = −(3γ − 4) N kB/(γ − 1), the table's C column.
  • It needs an ideal gas with γ above 4/3, and a contraction slow compared with the dynamical time, about half an hour for the Sun (4.25). A degenerate gas does not behave this way.
  • Uniform density and a constant L are simplifications. A real protostar is centrally condensed, which raises |Egrav| and T̄, and its luminosity changes as it shrinks.
See itWatch the end of a run at γ = 5/3, from its last few seconds. Watch for: Radius reaching 1.00 R⊙ with the mean temperature at 2.82 MK, and the run stopping there.
07

Summary

In one line. A star held up by gas pressure obeys one energy rule, the virial theorem, and that rule fixes both its mean temperature and how the energy it radiates is accounted for.

Key points

  • T̄ ∝ 1/R: a star that radiates contracts and gets hotter, so its heat capacity is negative.
  • At γ = 5/3, Etot = ½Egrav = −Eth: half the gravitational energy released is radiated and half heats the gas.
  • In general Etot = (3γ − 4)Egrav/3(γ − 1), so ΔEth/Erad = 1/(3γ − 4), and the star is loosely bound as γ → 4/3.
  • tKH = |Egrav|/2L is how long gravity alone can power the star.

Common mix-ups

  • "Losing energy cools the star." It makes the star contract. Stronger gravity needs faster particles, so the gas heats.
  • "All the gravitational energy released is radiated." At γ = 5/3 only half is, and at γ = 1.4 only a sixth. The rest heats the gas.
  • "A smaller star holds less heat, so T̄ falls." T̄ ∝ 1/R, and Eth rises as R falls.
  • "A brighter star radiates a larger share." L sets the speed of the contraction. γ sets the split.

Things to try on your own

  • Leave the radiation off and watch the readouts. Nothing changes, because the star only evolves while it radiates.
  • At each γ, note the clock when R reaches 5 R⊙ and compare it with the table.
  • At each γ, pause when Erad reads 1.000 and compare ΔEth with 1/(3γ − 4).
